beats.say: Hello! In the morning you see that your work mail sent forty emails abroad during the night.
Nobody had your password. A program stole your sign-in session, the cookie, from the browser.
The cookie tells the site you are already signed in, so it asks for no password and no code.
Three things help: a clean device, signing out of all sessions, and technical support.

scenes.prompt: What does each stolen item let a criminal do? Match them.

pairs.right: Get into the account without password or code
Get into your accounts on other sites
Read your chats and write as you

scenes.explain: A stealer takes all of these at once. So change every password, not just one, and close the sessions.

scenes.title: On a clean work computer
scenes.intro: You are on your work computer, and it is clean. Open your mail and choose the right step on each screen.

steps.label: Sent: tonight at 03:12, 40 emails to unknown addresses

actions.label: Call technical support
actions.feedback: Correct. A specialist can protect the account right away and see what was sent.

actions.label: Delete the emails
actions.feedback: Deleting does not bring back sent emails, but it destroys evidence. Tell technical support first.

actions.label: Close it, look later
actions.feedback: The attacker is still in the account and keeps writing. Every minute counts.

actions.label: This was not me
actions.feedback: Correct. The system marks the sign-in as suspicious, and technical support will see it.

actions.label: This was me
actions.feedback: You just confirmed the attacker's sign-in. Now the system treats them as you.

steps.say: The address is real and the computer is clean.

actions.label: Change password
actions.feedback: Correct. Type a new password only on a clean device, or the program takes that one too.

actions.label: Later
actions.feedback: The old password may be stolen. Change it now, from this clean computer.

steps.label: Active sessions: 3 devices. Sign out of all of them?

actions.label: Sign out of all devices
actions.feedback: Well done. The stolen cookie no longer works, and the attacker would have to sign in again.

actions.label: Later
actions.feedback: Changing the password does not always close an open session. The attacker may still be inside.

steps.label: New rule, 03:07: forward all mail to arxiv@poct-yedek.example

actions.label: Show the rule to technical support
actions.feedback: Correct. Even after the attacker left, this rule kept sending your mail to them.

actions.label: Leave it
actions.feedback: This is a hidden forward. Every new email you get will go to the attacker.

question.prompt: How did the attacker get into the mail without your password or code?

options.label: With a session stolen from the browser
options.feedback: Correct. The session shows the sign-in is already done, so no code is asked.

options.label: By guessing the password
options.feedback: Then the system would have asked for a code. Here neither a password nor a code was needed.

options.label: The mail server was hacked
options.feedback: The server is fine. What was stolen was the session in your browser.

scenes.explain: When a cookie is stolen, two-step verification does not help either. So do not let a stealer onto your computer.

scenes.prompt: If a computer is infected, put the steps in order.

items.label: Disconnect the infected computer from the network
Change passwords from a clean device
Let technical support rebuild the computer

scenes.explain: If you change a password on the infected computer, the program takes the new one too. The computer counts as clean only after a rebuild.

points: A stolen session gives access without password or code
Change passwords from a clean device, then sign out of all sessions
Let technical support rebuild the infected computer
